metadata.title: Tropical forest carbon: disturbance losses and recovery
metadata.description: Tropical forest degradation can remove substantial aboveground carbon even when forest remains. This synthesis of 146 studies compares losses after different disturbances and carbon stocks during recovery. After 20 years, recovering degraded forests averaged 75% of reference carbon stocks, versus 38% in secondary forests regrowing after clearance. The reference is prior standing or nearby undisturbed forest. This difference includes carbon retained after disturbance; it does not mean faster accumulation. The supplied loss and recovery workbooks contain the compiled study estimates and a reference crosswalk. They support comparisons for carbon accounting and recovery planning, with substantial variation among disturbance types, regions and studies; they are not predictions for a particular site.

evidence_summary.question: How much aboveground carbon is lost after different forms of tropical moist forest disturbance, and how do subsequent carbon stocks and accumulation differ between degraded forests and forests regrowing after clearance?
evidence_summary.finding: The meta-analysis synthesized 146 studies. Twenty years after the last disturbance, recovering degraded forests averaged (mean plus or minus one standard deviation) 75 ± 23% of reference aboveground carbon density (prior standing forest or nearby undisturbed forest), compared with 38 ± 16% for secondary regrowth forests. More intense and repeated disturbances were associated with greater losses. The paper reports faster accumulation as percentage points of reference stock during the first 20 years in secondary regrowth (+1.6 ± 0.8 percentage points per year) than in recovering degraded forest (+0.9 ± 0.7 percentage points per year).
evidence_summary.interpretation: Disturbance history matters for carbon accounting and recovery expectations. Higher stocks in recovering degraded forest partly reflect carbon that survived the disturbance. The reported percentages compare remaining or accumulated stocks with a reference of prior standing forest or nearby undisturbed forest; they are not the fraction of previously lost carbon recovered. These are synthesis estimates rather than a controlled test of a specific conservation intervention.
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Compiled study estimates underlying disturbance-loss and carbon-recovery comparisons.
limitations: Studies differ in disturbance history, timing, spatial scale and measurement methods; the synthesis is more geographically complete in tropical America than in Africa, Asia and Oceania.
The delivered workbooks contain 212 loss rows and 214 recovery rows, not one independent study per row. They are compiled inputs rather than new site observations or a spatial recovery forecast.
RefID 96 labels two citations; four in-preparation loss records lack cached RefID values. Original formulas and cached values are retained without recalculation.

metadata.title: Amazon fisheries: harvest trends and resilience
metadata.description: Amazon fish landings shifted toward smaller-bodied species across six regional time series, even though total landed biomass showed no consistent decline. The study combines these observations with food-web models in which species can temporarily replace declining catches, while continued depletion reduces that buffering capacity. The models suggest that higher biodiversity can delay fishery collapse; the landings alone do not demonstrate that outcome. This table provides 121 annual regional records from 1984–2016, including landings, diversity and biomass-weighted traits. It supports scrutiny of warning signs beyond total catch, but lacks fishing effort, subsistence harvests and independent stock surveys needed for a complete fishery assessment.

evidence_summary.question: Can changes in catch composition reveal declining resilience in multispecies fisheries when total catches do not clearly decline?
evidence_summary.finding: Across six Amazon landings series, landed biomass varied without a consistent downward trend, while mean body size declined and species composition changed. Evenness trends differed by region. In the theoretical food-web models, compensating species initially maintained harvests; continued depletion reduced compensation, and communities with fewer species reached collapse sooner under the modeled harvest targets.
evidence_summary.interpretation: Total landed biomass can conceal changes in the species supporting a fishery. The authors interpret composition, body-size and evenness patterns as warning signs consistent with exploitation and model-derived loss of resilience. Delayed collapse with higher biodiversity is a theoretical result, not an observed effect of a conservation intervention or a causal estimate from these regional tables.
evidence_summary.evidence_type: Observational landings analysis interpreted with theoretical food-web models
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Annual regional summary metrics from the observed landings series; not model trajectories or stock assessments.
limitations: Landings omit fishing effort and subsistence harvests. Market catches are not a complete census of fish communities, and other pressures can affect composition.
The theoretical results depend on harvest targets, community-level exploitation and modeled species interactions. Regional evenness trajectories are not interchangeable.
The prepared table contains annual summaries rather than taxon-level catches, model outputs or region geometries; the periods differ among regions.

Brazil: additional heat exposure under Amazon savannization
metadata.description: A worst-case climate-model experiment replacing all Amazon rainforest with savanna increased estimated human heat exposure, especially under high emissions. In the late-century RCP8.5 scenario, the study estimated more than 11 million additional people exposed to extreme in-shade heat stress, including about 5.7 million in highly vulnerable communities. These are conditional estimates using 2019 population, not forecasts of population growth or observed health outcomes. This table contains the 12 published Figure 3 estimates across historical and future climates, heat-exposure settings and vulnerability groups. It supports comparing the modeled human consequences of forest loss; the high-vulnerability figures are subsets of the totals and must not be added to them.

evidence_summary.question: How could replacement of all Amazon rainforest by savanna change human heat-stress exposure under historical and future climates, and who would be most vulnerable?
evidence_summary.finding: The worst-case experiment replacing all Amazon rainforest with savanna increased exposure to extreme heat stress. Under late-century RCP8.5, the paper reports more than 11 million additional people above the in-shade extreme-risk threshold relative to the forested scenario; about 5.7 million were in the high-vulnerability subset. Figure 3 reports additional exposure attributed to Amazon deforestation across historical, RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 climates, for in-shade and outdoor conditions.
evidence_summary.interpretation: These comparisons illustrate potential exposure consequences of complete Amazon rainforest replacement by savanna and their overlap with social vulnerability. The population is held at 2019 levels, so the results ask how that population would be exposed under the simulated climates. They do not predict a specific future deforestation trajectory, demographic change, illness or mortality. The published Figure 3 values are transcribed, not independently recomputed from the municipal inputs.
evidence_summary.evidence_type: Climate-model scenario experiment with population exposure analysis
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Published Figure 3 additional-exposure estimates, with municipal inputs retained as supporting data.
limitations: A particular climate model and complete Amazon rainforest replacement by savanna define this worst-case experiment; it does not represent ordinary partial deforestation, observed impacts or a calibrated forecast of a policy intervention.
Population growth, demographic changes and changes in adaptation are not modeled. Social vulnerability describes population context rather than a measured health response.

Population units are millions, and the high-vulnerability rows overlap the total-population rows. The paper gives inconsistent start years for its historical and future climate periods; categorical source labels are retained.

Eastern Amazon: biodiversity and carbon across land uses
metadata.description: Land-use comparisons at 310 eastern Amazon sites show that ecological losses extend beyond complete forest clearance. Logged-and-burned primary forest had 25% lower large-tree richness and 27% lower dung-beetle richness than undisturbed primary forest; aboveground carbon also differed substantially among forest conditions. These are observational comparisons used to estimate transition impacts, not repeated measurements of experimentally changed sites. The supplied table contains site-level richness for seven groups and four carbon pools, with forest-species richness linked separately. It supports examining which ecological components differ across land uses and why tracking forest area alone can miss degradation; it does not itself contain the paper’s estimated transition effects.

evidence_summary.question: How do different land-use and land-cover transitions compare in their ecological consequences, including changes within forests that remain standing?
evidence_summary.finding: Using 310 sites, the study compared biodiversity, carbon and soil across seven land-use classes and estimated impacts for 18 transitions. Logged-and-burned versus undisturbed primary forest had 25% lower large-tree richness and 27% lower dung-beetle richness. Aboveground carbon was 28–46% lower in logged or logged-and-burned forest than in undisturbed forest. Combining ecological contrasts with transition rates identified forest conversion to pasture as both prevalent and high impact.
evidence_summary.interpretation: The evidence supports examining degradation and regeneration alongside clearance, and evaluating biodiversity and carbon separately rather than treating forest area as a complete measure of condition. The comparisons are observational across sites, not before-and-after interventions. The delivered table is an input dataset of site aggregates; estimated transition effects, uncertainty and regional transition frequencies require the paper’s analyses and additional inputs.
evidence_summary.evidence_type: Observational site comparisons combined with land-cover transition analysis
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Site-level biodiversity and carbon inputs underlying comparisons among land-use classes.
limitations: The field sites are in two eastern Amazon regions and were surveyed during 2010–2011; results should not be read as a causal estimate applicable uniformly across Amazonia.
Missing values remain NA; orchid bees were sampled only in Paragominas. Forest species means species recorded at least once at a primary-forest site, not necessarily forest specialists.
Carbon is expressed per hectare, with soil carbon measured at 0–30 cm depth. Coordinates require a verified join and CRS before mapping.

metadata.title: Amazon tree diversity: plot observations
metadata.description: Amazon tree diversity varies strongly among forest types and regions, so tree counts or a single basin-wide average cannot describe it adequately. Using 2,046 inventory plots, the study found distinct patterns in density, species richness and Fisher’s alpha diversity, and used forest-type-specific spatial models to map those patterns. This table supplies the plot observations and standardized diversity measures behind that analysis, for free-standing woody stems at least 10 cm in diameter. It supports checking the observational basis of regional biodiversity comparisons. It is not a current forest-condition map or evidence of change through time; the supplied coordinates remain attributes because their datum is unverified.

evidence_summary.question: How do tree density, diversity and species richness vary across Amazonian forest types and regions, and what observations support the mapped patterns?
evidence_summary.finding: The study used 2,046 inventory plots and found strong variation among soil–forest combinations and regions. For example, Fisher’s alpha diversity was highest in terra-firme forests of the western Pebas region and French Guiana, with lower values in white-sand, floodplain and swamp settings. Forest type explained 23% of variation in plot Fisher’s alpha, while a combined spatial model explained 66% for that untransformed metric. These are descriptions and models of spatial variation rather than trends through time.
evidence_summary.interpretation: Plot measurements help distinguish density, richness and diversity and test the basis of regional biodiversity maps. Conservation comparisons require attention to forest type and species composition, not richness alone. The delivered table contains observations and derived plot metrics; regional interpolation, species distributions and current deforestation are separate products and analyses.
evidence_summary.evidence_type: Forest inventory observations with spatial modeling in the associated study
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Plot-level density, richness, diversity and reference data underlying regional models.
limitations: The observations concern undisturbed or old-growth forest inventories and stems with DBH at least 10 cm; they do not represent every vegetation state or all life stages.
All 2,046 supplied plots are retained, while individual modeling steps apply additional filters. Plot establishment year is not a measurement date or a repeated time series.

Coordinate datum remains unverified. The source includes three establishment years in 2021 although the paper describes coverage through 2020. Species richness per hectare and at 500 trees are derived standardizations, not raw species totals.

metadata.description: Animal seed dispersal is widespread among Amazonian trees: the study’s two classifications assign roughly four in five sampled species to animal-mediated dispersal. This highlights a potential dependence of forest regeneration on animals, rather than demonstrating a restoration response to protecting them. The supplied table contains dispersal assignments, seed-mass classes and fruit fleshiness for 5,201 species, keeping the two classifications separate. It supports comparisons of tree traits and potential dispersal dependencies; it is a selected part of the broader pollination-and-dispersal study, not its complete interaction network. Some species have multiple assignments, and the seed-mass values are class codes rather than measurements in grams.

evidence_summary.question: How widespread is animal-mediated seed dispersal among Amazonian trees, and how do seed and fruit traits differ among dispersal modes?
evidence_summary.finding: The paper’s Discussion summarizes 78–83% of the sampled species as animal dispersed, depending on classification, with arboreal vertebrates prominent. Animal-dispersed species generally have fleshy fruits. The analysis identifies a small set of abundant genera that contribute a disproportionate share of estimated fruit resources. The delivered table provides the underlying dispersal classifications and seed traits for 5,201 species; it does not include all pollination fields or population-weighted network calculations.
evidence_summary.interpretation: These trait assignments describe potential dependencies between trees and dispersers and help identify why animal loss could matter for regeneration. They do not measure changes in recruitment after animal loss or estimate the effect of a restoration intervention. Claims about combined pollination and dispersal dependence come from the broader study and cannot be reproduced from this selected dispersal table alone.
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Selected species-level dispersal assignments and seed traits from the broader network dataset.
limitations: The two classification systems use different categories and some species have multiple assignments; they should not be added together as independent species counts.
Dispersal assignments draw on literature and taxonomic inference, including genus-based assignments where appropriate; they are not all direct observations of interactions for each species.
The paper gives internally inconsistent exact counts/percentages in its dispersal Results; the summary uses its Discussion’s approximate range rather than silently resolving them.

Seed-mass values are logarithmic class codes, with exact class boundaries unresolved in the delivered metadata. The selected table alone does not reproduce pollination-network or population-weighted conclusions.

metadata.title: Full review evidence and source history
Chaglla hydropower: irrigation and climate scenarios
metadata.description: Upstream irrigation can protect crop production while reducing downstream hydropower in the upper Huallaga basin. Coupled watershed and reservoir models found that irrigation choices could affect Chaglla’s firm power more strongly than climate change alone, making food, energy and ecosystem objectives difficult to satisfy together. This table supplies 336 modeled mean- and firm-power summaries for 16 land-management configurations under selected climate scenarios. It supports inspecting the hydropower side of those comparisons; it is not the full multisector decision analysis or observed electricity generation. Original scenario codes are retained because their mapping and exact period bounds still need confirmation, as does the firm-power reliability criterion.
metadata.study_time: Historical and three future climatology groups; exact period bounds differ between the paper and supplied code.

evidence_summary.question: How do upstream land management and irrigation interact with climate change to affect Chaglla hydropower, and what trade-offs arise with food production and ecosystems?
evidence_summary.finding: In the modeled upper Huallaga system, maintaining current land use produced comparatively modest climate-only changes in hydropower, while irrigation expansion could substantially reduce firm power and create years with none. The broader analysis found that options favoring food production, hydropower or ecosystems separately could impose losses on other sectors, with more efficient irrigation and coordinated decisions reducing some trade-offs rather than eliminating them.
evidence_summary.interpretation: The evidence motivates considering upstream water use alongside reservoir operation when comparing adaptation options. These are conditional outcomes of a coupled modeling framework, not measured effects of implemented policies. The delivered table is a power-output subset with 16 management configurations and 21 KNN climate/model combinations each. It does not supply all crop, ecosystem, reservoir-operation or target-screening results from the 10,080-pathway decision analysis.
evidence_summary.evidence_type: Coupled watershed–reservoir modeling and climate/management scenario analysis
evidence_summary.dataset_role: Selected modeled mean/firm-power outputs; a subset of the broader multisector analysis.
limitations: Source management and climatology codes are preserved. Their complete mapping to published scenario names and precise time periods remains unresolved; the paper and code use differing period bounds.
The firm-power field is in MW, but its reliability/exceedance criterion was not established in the inspected paper, supplementary methods or supplied algorithms.

The analysis assumes management configurations remain constant within each climatic period; transitional effects, wider crop choices and future changes in electricity demand are not fully represented.

The prepared table contains modeled summary power, not measured generation or daily series, and retains only KNN results; the linked archive preserves the complete original KNN/BCSD tables and inspected scripts.
